THE COURSE

Beyond the
perfect market.

Standard microeconomics pictures rational agents with fixed preferences, full information, and costless exchange reaching efficient equilibria. Real economies work differently: preferences are shaped by experience, information is imperfect, transactions are costly, and contracts are always incomplete. Behind every functioning market lies an infrastructure of rules, norms, and organizations that standard theory takes for granted. This course builds the framework for understanding that infrastructure, in three parts. The first turns to foundations: why the standard assumptions of exogenous preferences, instrumental rationality, and perfect information are insufficient, and what replaces them. The second examines private governance: how firms, contracts, and hybrid arrangements organize exchange when markets alone cannot, through transaction costs, property rights, and the boundaries of the firm. The third develops the institutional framework: how formal and informal rules shape economic performance, why institutions differ across countries, and why they change so slowly. The course is analytical but discursive — no mathematical models — drawing on economics, political science, sociology, and history, and engaging directly with landmark work by Ronald Coase, Herbert Simon, Douglass North, Oliver Williamson, George Akerlof, and others.

Course Objectives

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • Explain why standard microeconomic assumptions are insufficient to understand real market economies, and the role of the institutional variable in economic life.

  • Identify and analyse a country's institutional framework — property rights, political rules, cultural norms — and how it shapes economic performance.

  • Apply transaction cost economics to contracting, the boundaries of the firm, and forms of economic organisation.

  • Evaluate the relationship between institutional design and economic development across national contexts.

  • Read and critically analyse scholarship in institutional and regulatory economics.

  • Present a research argument clearly and defend it under questioning.

These correspond to the competencies and learning outcomes of the verified course guide (GAUR): G001–G008, BC1–BC3, SC1–SC12, LO1–LO4.

Methodology

Why This Course Is Built Around Reading. Institutional economics is not learned by memorizing definitions, nor by consuming summaries. It is learned by reading complex material carefully, identifying causal mechanisms, weighing competing interpretations, and connecting evidence to argument. For this reason, the core methodological requirement of this course is reading.

Before you can analyze data, exercise judgment, think critically, or explain ideas coherently, you must first understand what others have argued, how they have argued it, and on what evidence. Reading is the entry point to all higher-order intellectual work. Without it, analysis becomes superficial, criticism becomes opinion, and explanation becomes empty rhetoric.

Reading cannot be delegated. The widespread adoption of AI tools has changed how students approach learning — but not how understanding is produced. Increasingly, students outsource reading to automated summaries and writing to text generators, which creates a false sense of comprehension: feeling informed without having processed the argument, the evidence, or the structure of the text itself. In economics or any serious professional field, you will be required to evaluate contradictory reports, detect manipulation in data presentation, synthesize information from multiple sources, and form independent, defensible judgments. These are human skills, developed only through sustained engagement with texts.

Lectures and seminars. The course combines lectures with student-led seminars. Lectures present the theoretical content of the three units in a discursive, analytical style, with no mathematical models. Seminars are devoted to the discussion of a pool of readings: each session includes several presentations, one reading per student, and all students are expected to take part in the discussion that follows. The readings are organised according to the three units, so how much weight each unit receives in the seminars depends on which readings students choose. If the distinction between the two formats is new to you, this short guide from Warwick Business School explains it well.

Slides are NOT distributed and no lecture notes are supplied. PowerPoint supports the explanation; it does not replace it. What matters is the argument as it is built in the room—attend and take your own notes.

Mobile phones are not to be used in class, whether during lectures or seminars. The only exception is a genuine emergency. If you need to use your phone because of an emergency, please notify the professor and, where appropriate, leave the classroom to deal with the situation. Except in such circumstances, the use of a mobile phone during class constitutes a serious breach of the course rules and will result in failing the course, with a final grade of 0.

Laptops and tablets may be used only for note-taking and for consulting the reading under discussion, and for no other purpose.

For a short reflection on the use of mobile phones in the classroom, read this piece from The Invisible Band of Economic Historians—it might make you reconsider how you use your phone in class.

Assessment

First Call (Ordinary). Students may choose between two pathways:

Option A — Continuous assessment. Seminar presentation (30%) + final exam (70%). Students present one reading from the seminar pool during the final nine sessions (27 Nov – 18 Dec) and sit the final exam. To pass, a mark of at least 5.0/10 in the exam is required before the seminar mark is added. The exam consists of three questions and students on this pathway answer two of them, choosing themselves which one to leave out: the skipped question is not graded and does not affect the other two. Attendance at every seminar session is compulsory and a register is taken. Informed participation in the discussion of other students' presentations may be recognised in the final grade at the professor's discretion, over and above the 30/70 split — this applies to continuous-assessment students only.

Option B — Final examination only. Final exam worth 100%, available to all students regardless of seminar participation. Students choosing this option must submit the course waiver form within the first nine weeks; continuous assessment is the default, so a student who does not submit it is taken to be following continuous assessment. Option B students answer all three exam questions and all three are graded: the right to leave one out belongs to continuous-assessment students only. Seminar attendance is not required, though it is recommended, and the grade is based on the exam alone.

What the final exam covers. The lecture content and the required textbook — Ménard and Shirley's Advanced Introduction to New Institutional Economics (Edward Elgar, 2022) — which the professor works from across the semester. Readings presented by fellow students are not examinable. If few students take up continuous assessment, the professor selects readings from the pool to fill the remaining seminar sessions and presents them himself; those readings are examinable for everyone and will be announced in advance in class and on eGela.

Second Call (Extraordinary). The same two options apply; the seminar presentation grade from the first call is retained.

Exam dates. First call: 13 January 2027, 10:00. Second call: 16 June 2027, 10:00.

Seminar Readings

The readings are available on this website, under Readings: one required textbook for every student, plus a pool of 41 texts for the seminar presentations. The textbook — Ménard and Shirley's Advanced Introduction to New Institutional Economics (Edward Elgar, 2022) — is available online through the EHU library, and a printed copy of the volume can be collected from the Penter copy shop at Sarriko.

Continuous-assessment students present one reading from the pool. Readings are claimed on eGela, where a list shows which are still free — claiming a reading there is how a student takes up continuous assessment. One reading, one student, first come, first served: once a reading is claimed it is gone, and a selection is final and cannot be changed afterwards, so read the abstract and choose carefully.

Selection closes at the end of Week 9 (6 November 2026), the same deadline as the course waiver, so that both decisions are made together. Claiming early is strongly advised: the pool shrinks as readings are taken, and an early choice leaves time to read the article properly and prepare the presentation. Students who have neither waived continuous assessment nor claimed a reading by the deadline will be assigned one by the professor.

Presentation format. Several presentations per session, each a minimum of 15 minutes, longer where the session allows. Cover: (a) research question and main argument; (b) theoretical framework and methodology; (c) key evidence or reasoning; (d) your own critical evaluation. Open Q&A after each presentation.

Statement On Cheating And Plagiarism

Cheating, plagiarism or otherwise obtaining grades under false pretenses constitute academic dishonesty according to the code of this university. University of the Basque Country (EHU) has a ZERO-TOLERANCE POLICY on cheating.

Cheating is defined as fraud, deceit, or dishonesty in an academic assignment. In any examinations, cheating includes using or attempting to use materials, or assisting others in using materials that are prohibited or inappropriate during an exam. The following situations are considered to be cheating: copying or attempting to copy from others during an exam; communicating answers with another person during an exam; using unauthorized materials, prepared answers, written notes, or concealed information during an exam; taking an exam for another person or having someone take an exam for you (Euskal Herriko Unibertsitatea, n.d.).

One of the most common forms of cheating is plagiarism, using another's words or ideas without proper citation. This includes submitting AI-generated text as your own work. Academic dishonesty will not be tolerated and penalties can include giving a 0 for the course or for the assignment.

Readings

required reading

Ménard, C., & Shirley, M. M. (Eds.) (2022). Advanced Introduction to New Institutional Economics. Edward Elgar.

The textbook is available as a digital copy through the EHU library; access requires logging in with your EHU ID. A printed copy of the volume can also be collected from the Penter copy shop at Sarriko—ask for the folder containing the reading for Institutions and Economic Regulation.

Price for the complete volume: €10.15 without binding and €12.55 with binding.

The volume can also be printed in separate parts rather than as a complete volume. Whatever option you prefer, please ask directly at Penter.

Seminars

Seminars are devoted to the close reading and discussion of key texts in institutional and regulatory economics. Students who choose continuous assessment each present one reading from the pool below.

Every reading on this page is a link. Click the author and year to open the text.

Access. Some of these readings are open access on the journal's own website — the Journal of Economic Perspectives, for instance, publishes everything free of charge — and will open straight away. Others are published behind a paywall and are linked through the EHU library, so you will be asked to sign in with your university credentials (your library ID) before the text appears. If a link offers to sell you the article, you are not signed in — go back through the library portal rather than paying for anything. Most of the pool is available digitally, but a few items are held only as physical copies, for consultation on the library premises; plan for that if you claim one of them. If a reading will not open for you, contact the EHU library services — they handle off-campus access and credential problems.

How It Works

  • One reading, one student. Each reading may be claimed by one student only, on a first-come, first-served basis via eGela, where a list shows which readings are still free. Claiming a reading there is how you take up continuous assessment.

  • A claim is final. Once a reading is taken it leaves the list and cannot be swapped. Open the text and read the abstract before you claim it.

  • Deadline: end of Week 9 (6 November 2026)—the same deadline as the course waiver, so that both decisions are made together. Claiming early is strongly advised: the pool shrinks as readings are taken, and an early choice leaves time to read the article properly and prepare. Students who have neither waived continuous assessment nor claimed a reading by the deadline will be assigned one by the professor.

  • Sessions. Seminars run in the final nine sessions of the course, 27 November – 18 December. Each session includes several presentations of a minimum of 15 minutes each, followed by open Q&A.

  • What is examinable and what is not. The lecture content and textbook material are examinable. The readings in the seminar pool, including those presented by fellow students, are NOT examinable. However, if only a small number of students opt for continuous assessment, the Professor may present selected readings from the pool himself. Only those readings presented by the Professor will become examinable for everyone, and they will be announced in advance.

The seminar schedule will be posted here as the course progresses.

seminar Presentation pool

For continuous assessment students only. Forty-one readings are organised by unit and alphabetically within each unit. Selection is open across all three units. Reading selection will be made via the eGela platform.

About Me

Iker Saitua is an associate professor in the Department of Public Policy and Economic History at the University of the Basque Country, where he teaches economic history and institutional economics. He earned his PhD from the University of Nevada, Reno (2016) and held a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of California, Riverside. His research applies institutional economics to the economic history of the American West and of Central America, with particular attention to markets, property rights, and institutional change. He is the author of Basque Immigrants and Nevada's Sheep Industry (University of Nevada Press, 2019) and the forthcoming Sheeptopia: Making the Sheep Industry in the American West, 1870–1920 (University of Oklahoma Press).
